name: Bannack State Park
summary: It marks the site of the state's first major gold strike in 1862 and is one of Montana’s best-preserved abandoned settlements. You can walk right into over 50 standing log and frame buildings lining Main Street.

name: Garnet Ghost Town
summary: Tucked up in the Garnet Range just an hour outside Missoula, this 1890s gold camp operates as a prime historical preservation site. Over 30 intact log cabins, hotels, and commercial buildings deliver an authentic, raw look at frontier mining life. You can walk through the Wells Hotel and Kelly's Saloon without behind-the-glass barriers.

name: Granite Ghost Town
summary: Located near Philipsburg, this 1890s silver boomtown requires a steep, winding drive up the mountain. The payoff is a rugged high-elevation ruins site featuring the stone walls of the old Miners Union Hall and the superintendent's house. It delivers incredible photography and striking vistas of the Flint Creek Valley.

name: Virginia City
summary: Paired closely with nearby Nevada City, this historic territorial capital operates like a living museum. Virginia City retains a handful of full-time residents and runs live tourist performances, historic train rides, and preserved 1860s storefronts. Nearly half the structures predate 1900, making it an unmatched walk through the Alder Gulch gold rush.

name: Nevada City
summary: Sitting just a mile and a half down the road from Virginia City, this sister camp houses one of the largest collections of original 19th-century frontier buildings in the West. Over 100 historic structures and tens of thousands of artifacts fill the outdoor museum grounds. During summer weekends, living history interpreters bring the old cabins and music hall back to life.

name: Elkhorn State Park
summary: Unlike rowdy single-miner camps, this 1880s silver town in the Elkhorn Mountains was home to married miners and their families. Today it serves as Montana's smallest state park, anchored by two remarkable wood-frame buildings: Fraternity Hall and Gillian Hall. These ornate false-front showpieces stand side-by-side among private cabins and quiet mountain timber.

name: Comet
summary: Once the richest operation in its district, the Comet Mine pulled over $20 million in silver, lead, zinc, and gold from the hills near Boulder. Today, a sprawling 200-foot concentrator mill and dozens of weathered frame houses dominate the dry gulch. It is one of the largest semi-intact ghost towns in the region, though the deteriorating structures must be viewed with caution.

name: Marysville
summary: Perched in the mountains northwest of Helena near the Great Divide ski area, this former gold capital once boasted 4,000 residents and the famous Drumlummon Mine. Tumbling historic wooden buildings now mix with a stubborn group of current residents and the classic Marysville House restaurant. The old mining camp refuses to fade away completely, giving visitors a blend of living town and rugged ruins.

name: Coloma
summary: Hidden deep in the woods just a couple miles from Garnet, this mysterious 1890s gold camp sits quietly off the beaten path. While few standing structures remain compared to its famous neighbor, overgrown foundations, collapsed cabins, and archaeological test sites dot the forest floor. University of Montana researchers regularly study the site to uncover how isolated mountain miners lived.

name: Rimini
summary: Founded as a gold and silver camp in 1864 down a narrow gulch southwest of Helena, this tucked-away settlement sits right beneath the landmark Red Mountain. Beyond its mining boom, the town gained a unique chapter in history during World War II when the nearby Camp Rimini trained military sled dogs and pack mules. Weathered cabins still hug the creek bed alongside a handful of occupied homes.

name: Castle Town
summary: Tucked under the Castle Mountains, this 1880s silver and lead boomtown once packed 80 dwellings, 14 saloons, and seven brothels into its mountain clearing. Legendary frontier figure Calamity Jane even tried running a restaurant here before the 1893 Silver Panic crashed the local economy. Dozens of greying log cabins and false-front buildings still stand in the open meadow.

name: Kendall
summary: Carved into the North Moccasin Mountains of Fergus County, this early 20th-century gold camp stood out because many of its core buildings were built from native cut stone rather than hasty timber. The mines produced millions in gold and helped pioneer cyanide processing in the region before shutting down around 1920. Visitors can still see the crumbling stonework of the old bank and commercial foundations.

name: Zortman
summary: Nestled in the Little Rocky Mountains of Phillips County, this remote camp grew around philanthropist Pete Zortman's Alabama gold mine and limestone crusher. Today it operates as a quiet semi-ghost town where historic log structures, an old white church, and mining remnants sit beside a small modern community. It serves as an authentic basecamp for exploring the surrounding island mountain range.

name: Bearmouth
summary: Located along the Clark Fork River east of Missoula, this settlement wasn't a mining camp itself, but the vital supply hub and stagecoach stop for Garnet and Beartown. Miners hauled their gold and silver ore down the canyon to Bearmouth for smelting and river ferry transport along the Mullan Road. The historic two-story stagecoach inn and massive livery stable still stand beside the interstate.

name: Giltedge
summary: High in the Judith Mountains near Lewistown, this major gold camp pioneered open-pit cyanide extraction in the 1890s and peaked at 1,500 residents. Calamity Jane frequented its saloons during its boom years while surrounding mines pulled roughly 100,000 ounces of gold from the hills. You can drive the public county roads past the surviving stone storefront, wooden jail, and brick ruins.

name: Gold Creek
summary: Sitting off Interstate 90 between Missoula and Garrison, this peaceful hamlet marks the documented site of Montana's very first gold discovery by Francois Finlay ('Benetsee') in 1852. That initial find and the 1858 Stuart brothers strike kicked off the prospecting fever that reshaped the territory. A few weathered historic buildings and pioneer markers remain in the quiet ranching community.

name: Independence
summary: High in the Absaroka Range south of Big Timber, this remote gold camp is now a landscape of cabin and mining remnants. Its mountain setting makes it a destination for those interested in Montana’s mining past. Check current road conditions and access before planning a trip.

name: Glendale
summary: During the 1880s silver boom, 2,000 people lived in this remarkably civilized canyon town near Melrose while three 50-ton blast furnaces roared day and night. The district produced roughly $20 million in silver bars before the mines closed in 1900. Today, a towering brick smelter smokestack, charcoal kilns, and stone foundations rise out of the sagebrush down the dirt canyon road.

name: Hecla
summary: Located further up the mountain road past the Glendale smelters in the Pioneer Mountains, this high-altitude glacial basin produced the raw silver and lead ore that fed the valley furnaces. Miners braved brutal winters at 8,500 feet to work the Lion Mountain tunnels until the veins played out. Scattered cabin ruins, stone walls, and mine dumps reward drivers who make the climb.

name: Diamond City
summary: Founded in 1864 by former Confederate soldiers in Confederate Gulch, this camp yielded some of the richest placer gold per acre in world history. At its peak, cowboy artist Charlie Russell called it the most perfect mining camp in Montana. Subsequent hydraulic mining literally washed the hillside away, leaving only a historic cemetery, massive tailings piles, and a few cabin remnants.
